decisions.quote: Multilab Direct Replication of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966): Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age
decisions.location: title, line 1 (see also reference list, line 142)
decisions.reason: The paper is a multilab direct replication of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966), 'Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age', Child Development, 37(2), 283-299. Both the shipped row (input_row_index 880) and blind target 0 identify this exact same original article; the pairing flag (conflicting_dois) arose only because the shipped record uses the Wiley publisher DOI (10.1111/j.1467-8624.1966.tb05387.x) whereas the blind coding extracted the JSTOR DOI printed in the reference list (10.2307/1126804).

decisions.quote: Specifically, this contemporary replication examined Flavell et al.’s findings in geographically diverse international samples to determine if the original findings are generalizable to modern data collection techniques (e.g. computerized task presentation).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind classify the study as a 'replication'. The authors collected new empirical data from 977 child participants across 17 laboratories following a modernized version of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky's (1966) experimental protocol to re-test the original findings.

decisions.quote: Work by Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966) indicated a change in the spontaneous production of overt verbalization behaviors when comparing young children (age 5) to older children (age 10). Despite the critical role that this evidence of a change in verbalization behaviors plays in modern theories of cognitive development and working memory, there has only been one other published near-replication of this work (Keeney, Cannizzo, & Flavell, 1967). This Registered Replication Report relied upon 17 labs who contributed their results to a larger and more comprehensive sample of children. We assessed memory performance and the presence or absence of verbalization behaviors of young children at different ages, and determined that the original pattern of findings was largely upheld: older children were more likely to verbalize, and their memory spans improved. We confirmed that 5- and 6-year-old children who verbalized recalled more than children who did not verbalize. However, unlike Flavell et al., substantial proportions of our 5- and 6-year-old samples overtly verbalized at least sometimes during the picture memory task. Also, continuous increase in overt verbalization from 7- to 10-years-old was not consistently evident in our samples. These robust findings should be weighed when considering theories of cognitive development, particularly theories concerning when verbal rehearsal emerges and relations between speech and memory.
decisions.location: Independent parent full primary-source inspection; final_v2_context_0125 passage 880_abstract
decisions.reason: Parent applies Codebook Step3rule1 to the authors' whole-replication synthesis: after describing the multi-lab assessment of memory and verbalization, the Abstract says the original pattern of findings was largely upheld; the whole Discussion says the general pattern was upheld and the closing synthesis says this multi-lab study replicated the spirit of the original findings. This is a study-level assessment of the developmental pattern and speech-memory relation, not an isolated significant effect. Rule1does not demand an unqualified/all-components success statement. The explicit greater young-child verbalization and unconfirmed7–10increase remain reported contrasts; they do not override that author overall assessment. No claim of a demonstrated7–10decrease or absolute refutation is made, and missing table cells are not reconstructed. The final expert's mixed opinion and invalid spliced quotation are preserved, with this explicit parent hierarchy decision superseding them; this is not acceptance/repair of the raw quotation.
decisions.parent_material_interpretation: Overall-author priority: same rule as row2009; retain component contrasts rather than mechanically count them.
